claims.text: Atomic-size differences among constituent elements increase local diffusion activation barriers in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Higher local diffusion barriers kinetically suppress diffusion-driven segregation and clustering.
Kinetic suppression of diffusion maintains a homogeneous solid solution despite a thermodynamic drive for chemical ordering.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy nanoalloy with only slight nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
Atomic-size mismatch can be deliberately varied while retaining compositionally similar alloys and high configurational entropy.
Diffusion is active over approximately 0.5–0.9 times the melting temperature without necessarily overcoming the proposed barriers completely.
Pair-correlation functions and evolving short-range-order or clustering patterns can track local atomic diffusion events.
Chemical complexity and local chemical fluctuations in compositionally complex alloys produce a spectrum of diffusion activation barriers.
Regions with more pronounced atomic-size differences have higher activation energies for atomic jumps.
Reduced atomic mobility limits the development and growth of segregated clusters.
High-entropy alloys can develop chemical clustering and short-range ordering at elevated temperatures.
Nanoalloys with larger atomic-size differences will have lower diffusion coefficients than low-mismatch alloys under the same thermal conditions.
Nanoalloys with larger atomic-size differences will exhibit less early clustering and remain more homogeneous at high temperature.
Low-size-mismatch high-entropy nanoalloys undergo faster diffusion, greater segregation, and more pronounced local chemical ordering.
The proposed size-mismatch mechanism dominates between roughly 50% and 90% of the melting temperature when configurational entropy remains high.
The mechanism may cease to apply when temperature is too low for appreciable diffusion or high enough to overcome the elevated barriers.
HRTEM, atom-probe tomography, and molecular-dynamics simulations can characterize clustering, local composition, and structural evolution at nanometer scales.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes compositionally similar alloys, but the experiment requires identical overall compositions with different atomic-size mismatch. For a fixed set of elements and atomic fractions, the conventional composition-based size-mismatch parameter is fixed, so the stated comparison cannot vary mismatch independently without changing composition or defining another way to alter effective atomic sizes.
